additions.reason: The Rebbe closes the Torah with an explicit bechina-language equation: 'וְזֶהוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל – רָאשֵׁי-תֵבוֹת: אֵל שַׁדַּי יִתֵּן לָכֶם רַחֲמִים'. The word 'וְזֶהוּ' (and this IS) is a bechina marker — it equates Israel with the acrostic expressing God's gift of compassion. In this Torah, ישראל IS the concept of received compassion; the name itself encodes the divine giving of mercy into human hands. This makes ישראל a bechina of the Package 1 cluster (רחמנות / שהשם יתברך יתן לנו הרחמנות). It is not currently in the bechina dataset for this Torah.
additions.source_quote: וְזֶהוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל – רָאשֵׁי-תֵבוֹת: אֵל שַׁדַּי יִתֵּן לָכֶם רַחֲמִים, כַּנַּ"ל, כִּי הָרַחֲמָנוּת נַעֲשָׂה עַל-יְדֵי מַסְעֵי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּנַּ"ל

additions.reason: The Torah repeatedly uses 'פגם עבודה זרה' (the blemish/damage of idolatry) as the full concept being atoned for. While it appears as an eitza node in the dataset (in 'כשנתכפר פגם עבודה זרה'), it is closely related to 'עבודה זרה' as the state or damage of idolatry — essentially a bechina of the same evil domain. The Rebbe's language 'יֵשׁ פְּגַם עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה' treats it as a substantive concept in the same cluster as corruption of faith and turning away from God.
additions.source_quote: כִּי אֲפִלּוּ כְּשֶׁאֵין עוֹבְדִין עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, יֵשׁ פְּגַם עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה

analysis_notes.data_quality_note: Two node IDs for the same concept appear in the bechina edges: 'עבודה  זרה' (double space, in edge B2) and 'עבודה זרה' (single space, in edge B3). These represent the same concept. The double-space variant appears to be a data-entry artifact. Both are assigned to Package 2.
analysis_notes.good_evil_mirror: Package 1 (רחמנות — compassion) is the good pole; Package 2 (עבודה זרה — idolatry/turning away) is its evil mirror. The Torah's single eitza argument flows from the evil package to the good: atonement of idolatry's blemish → sweetening of divine anger → flow of compassion. The journeys of Israel (מסעי בני ישראל) are the eitza mechanism connecting the evil package to the good one.
